Does disinfecting every hospital surface prevent more infections?

A randomized study of 13,896 patients found no superiority of routine disinfection over soap-based or probiotic cleaning on non-ICU wards.

A hospital room is not just walls and furniture. Its cleaning regime is part of the built environment. But does stronger routine disinfection actually prevent more infections?

The study

At Charité Berlin, 18 non-intensive-care wards (10 surgical and 8 medical) rotated through three randomized cleaning strategies between June 2017 and August 2018: soap-based cleaner, disinfectant, and a Bacillus-based probiotic cleaner. Each ward used each strategy for four months of observation, preceded by a one-month wash-in period. The primary outcome was hospital-acquired infections, not microbiome diversity or neurological health.

The numbers

Among 13,896 eligible patients, 4,708 were exposed to soap-based cleaning, 4,535 to disinfection, and 4,653 to probiotic cleaning. Infection rates per 1,000 exposure days were 2.31, 2.21, and 2.21, respectively. Compared with soap, the incidence-rate ratio was 0.95 for disinfection (95% CI 0.69–1.31; p=0.953) and 0.96 for probiotic cleaning (95% CI 0.69–1.32; p=0.955). Neither strategy showed statistically significant superiority.

Architectural implications

Infection prevention depends on how buildings are operated as well as how they are designed. For routine cleaning on these wards, the data challenge the assumption that more chemical disinfection necessarily yields fewer infections. This does not argue against targeted disinfection when clinically required.

Limits and conclusion

This was a single-centre study in non-ICU wards, not a test of intensive-care units, outbreaks, or home cleaning. Confidence intervals leave room for clinically relevant differences; no significant difference is not proof of equivalence. The study did not measure brain outcomes, epigenetics, or changes in the indoor microbiome.
